title: The Turtle Ship
tagline: With 13 ships he defeated 333 — and saved Korea.

scenes.text: Korea, 1592. Japan's Toyotomi Hideyoshi launches an invasion with 160,000 soldiers. The Korean army collapses. Only the navy — commanded by Admiral Yi Sun-sin — holds.
Yi has already prepared. His turtle ship — the geobukseon — is iron-plated, arrow-proof, and fitted with cannons on all sides. The Japanese have never seen anything like it.

challenge.question: What was the decisive ratio of ships at the Battle of Myeongnyang (1597), which Admiral Yi Sun-sin won?
options: 13 Korean ships against approximately 333 Japanese warships
challenge.fact: At Myeongnyang in 1597, Admiral Yi commanded just 13 remaining warships against a Japanese fleet of over 300. He positioned his ships in the narrow strait where the current reversed twice daily, luring the Japanese into a bottleneck where numbers meant nothing. He sank or damaged 31 enemy ships without losing a single one of his own.

scenes.text: Battle of Hansan Island: Yi lures the Japanese fleet into open water with a crane-wing formation. 59 Japanese ships are sunk or captured. Korea's southern sea is saved.

challenge.statement: Admiral Yi Sun-sin was never removed from command during the Japanese invasions.
challenge.fact: Yi was arrested, tortured, and demoted twice — the victim of court intrigue and a Japanese deception operation that planted false intelligence to undermine him. He served as a common soldier before being hastily reinstated when the navy collapsed without him. Myeongnyang was fought with the 13 ships that remained after his absence.

scenes.text: He is falsely accused by jealous officials, tortured, stripped of rank. He fights the next campaign as a common soldier — still winning battles.

challenge.question: Arrange the key events of the Imjin War and Yi Sun-sin's role in order:
items: Japan invades Korea with 150,000 troops — the army sweeps north in weeks
Yi wins the Battle of Okpo — the first Korean naval victory of the war
The turtle ship is deployed at Sacheon — its iron-clad deck deflects Japanese muskets
Yi is arrested on false charges and demoted — the Korean navy is destroyed without him
Yi is reinstated with 13 ships and wins the Battle of Myeongnyang
Yi is killed by a stray bullet at the Battle of Noryang — his last victory, his last breath
challenge.fact: Yi Sun-sin died at Noryang in 1598 — struck by a bullet during the battle that would finally expel Japanese forces from Korea. His last words, reportedly, were: 'The battle is at its height — do not announce my death.' He won the battle from his deathbed, concealing his death until the Japanese had fled.

scenes.text: Battle of Myeongnyang, 1597: 13 Korean ships vs 333 Japanese. Yi positions his fleet in a narrow strait where tides neutralize numbers. He wins — arguably the greatest naval victory in history.

challenge.instruction: Korean resistance against invasion required total commitment. Command the naval engagement — read the current, hold the strait, and let geography be your fleet.
challenge.fact: The turtle ship (geobukseon) was the world's first ironclad warship — its curved, iron-plated deck prevented Japanese boarding parties from swarming the deck in their preferred hand-to-hand style. It carried cannons on all sides and a dragon's head at the bow that could emit smoke to disorient the enemy. Yi deployed it as a spearhead to break enemy formations before his lighter warships engaged.

scenes.text: He is killed at the final battle of Noryang — the war won, Korea saved. His last words: 'Do not let them know I am dead.' The battle continued. Korea survived.

challenge.instruction: At Hansan Island, Yi surrounded the Japanese fleet using the 'Crane Wing' formation — a classic envelopment. Execute the maneuver: extend the wings, close the trap, allow no escape.
challenge.fact: The Battle of Hansan Island (1592) is considered one of the most significant naval battles in Asian history. Yi used a feigned retreat to draw the Japanese fleet into open water, then sprang the crane-wing encirclement. He sank 47 Japanese ships and captured 12, breaking Japan's naval dominance in a single afternoon.

challenge.instruction: Yi studied Sun Tzu as carefully as he studied tides. Deploy your forces where terrain, timing, and surprise multiply every ship's effectiveness.
challenge.fact: Yi's battle reports, collected in his Nanjung Ilgi (War Diary), are among the most detailed military documents of the 16th century. He recorded his tactics, his anxieties, his observations of weather and tide, and his grief. The diary survived the war hidden under floorboards. It is now a Korean national treasure.
